title: Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs
author: The Register AI
contentSnippet: The Ubuntu Summit isn't all about Ubuntu, or even Linux. The second day opened with a talk from CrossPoint Reader project lead Justin Mitchell, with both good and bad news for all kinds of FOSS. The talk, EPUBs, ESP32s, and Everyone's A Developer Now, was all about a FOSS project that isn't Linux-based – because the devices it targets are much too small to run even the smallest, most cut-down distro. Recently, a new generation of roughly credit-card sized ebook readers has been thriving. Some have integral magnets, which let them cling to the back of iPhones – or to models with magnetically attached wireless chargers, anyway. The idea is that instead of waking your phone and doom-scrolling, you flip it over and read a book. They are bringing about what Mitchell calls "the Tiktok-ification of reading." Many of them, though, come from their various manufacturers significantly limited by their original OSes. The strong sales are linked to the availability of free, open-source, cross-platform alternative firmware, which removes many of the restrictions that the devices ship with. For most of them, that means Crosspoint Reader. Some devices are now shipping, new, with versions of Crosspoint Reader. This runs on multiple different models of compact e-readers, and this small community project has seen impressively widespread adoption: over 300,000 installations. Early in his talk, project lead Mitchell mentioned more than 1,600 forks on GitHub, but at the time of writing, that's up to 2,300 and counting. He estimates nearly half a million users. This kind of success forced Crosspoint Reader to change from being FOSS code to a product. A peripheral example is the Brick Club List, a list of what versions work with what devices – an Excel spreadsheet that grew into a website. If you haven't been paying attention, you may not have noticed just how much e-readers have shrunk – in size and in cost – in the last few years. The Reg FOSS desk first noticed this trend in 2024, when we read about the smartphone-sized Onyx Palma, which sold for around $300 (about £225). As it happens, this was a decade after The Register first looked at one of Boox's devices. Mini e-readers – and their prices – have continued shrinking since. title: How LoanPro built an agentic AI loan servicing assistant with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Mariah Miller
contentSnippet: This post is co-written with Mariah Miller from AWS and Colin Terry from LoanPro Have you ever wondered what the experience is like for the person on the other end of the phone when you call your bank for support? When a borrower calls a lender, the answering agent must pull account data from dozens of fields, transaction histories, and workflow queues to orient themselves before they can help the borrower. title: Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams
author: Mia Chang
contentSnippet: Companies build agentic AI platforms to govern the applications, tools, skills, models, and storage that agents use. The nondeterministic nature of generative AI models introduces a complexity that previous software development practices didn’t anticipate. Consider a real estate app that generates property listings from retrieved data: does it accurately reflect the property, or hallucinate features that don’t exist? Or a customer service agent grounded on internal knowledge bases: can you verify that it doesn’t surface confidential information? Until recently, responsible AI (RAI) was model-centric, scoped to the machine learning development lifecycle: training, testing, and inference. Models didn’t reason, use tools, or take actions. When the conversation extended to model-powered systems, it covered statistically bounded situations you could test against known inputs. Generative AI powered applications and agents changed this. The systems now reason, act, compose tools dynamically, and interact over multiple steps, expanding both the scope and the depth of what responsible AI must cover. Organizations are turning Responsible AI, which includes the pillars of security and privacy, veracity and robustness, fairness, safety, controllability, explainability, transparency, and governance into a growth strategy by addressing its expanding scope early. When enterprises adopt agentic AI at scale, the positive and negative impacts come hand in hand. As Wade and Wirtz observe in the Harvard Business Review , trust is becoming a competitive differentiator. The same capabilities that personalize at scale can also surveil and discriminate, and organizations that govern them earn stakeholder confidence. Robinhood, for example, built a generative AI financial crimes agent on Amazon Bedrock with strict data governance. They achieved a 20% efficiency gain while maintaining regulatory compliance. Structuring these practices across platform maturity is the next step. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Application teams. Application teams, sometimes called Workstream teams, build and own agents on the platform. title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide . title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation
author: Deokhyung Kang
contentSnippet: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.

title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.” Read full article Comments

title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
author: Brian Caulfield
contentSnippet: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases. SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide]. Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens. title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
author: Dina Genkina
contentSnippet: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue?

title: A Full-Ledger Counterfactual Audit of Adaptive Reasoning
author: Xiaopeng Chu
contentSnippet: Adaptive reasoning must decide whether to answer now or spend more compute. Predicting that the current answer is wrong does not establish whether further reasoning will improve it. We introduce the Full-Ledger Counterfactual Value Audit (FLCVA), which compares an immediate answer with four fixed-length continuations from the same frozen prefix under one answer procedure and accounts for the cost of every signal used by a policy. On GSM8K and MATH-500, a random 256-token continuation recovers a wrong answer in 26.6% of Qwen3-8B cases and 18.9% of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B cases, while damaging a correct answer in 1.4% and 1.9%. Correctness labels from independently sampled continuations predict a separate continuation's outcome in both primary models. In offline replay, using these labels to allocate compute improves performance on DeepSeek; the Qwen3 gain remains inconclusive. Under full cost accounting, the tested lightweight, myopic controllers mainly recognize current errors and add little continuation-specific value beyond that shortcut. A Llama-8B replication and action/cost ablations examine the robustness of these findings. FLCVA separates measuring local continuation value, predicting it from observable signals, and using those predictions to allocate computation.

title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
author: Joshua Adrian Cahyono
contentSnippet: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.

title: Understand How Satellite Links Shape IoT Device Design and Testing
author: Anritsu
contentSnippet:
Download this complimentary White Paper today!

This White Paper explains how satellite access in 5G changes the design and testing of IoT devices. It shows why realistic satellite conditions are essential for reliable field performance.

How 3GPP Releases 15, 16, and 17 brought satellite access into 5G NR, NB-IoT, and eMTC.

Why satellite links suit IoT devices that send small, infrequent, and delay-tolerant messages.

Where non-terrestrial networks (NTN) add value, including asset tracking, agriculture, public safety, and offshore operations.

How power efficiency, RF signaling, and antenna design shape satellite-connected device development.

Why long propagation delay, Doppler shift, and intermittent coverage make static test methods insufficient.

Which measurements show deployment readiness, such as transmit power, modulation accuracy, spectral emissions, receiver sensitivity, and block error rate (BLER).

How emulated satellite conditions help verify synchronization, signaling, HARQ behavior, mobility, and interoperability.

Click ‘LOOK INSIDE’ to Download Now. IEEE Spectrum and Wiley are proud to bring you this White Paper, sponsored by Anirtsu More Information Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

summary.tldr:
Anritsu has released a white paper detailing the integration of satellite access into 5G standards via 3GPP Releases 15, 16, and 17. The document focuses on the technical requirements for Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN), which enable 5G NR, NB-IoT, and eMTC connectivity for devices in remote areas where terrestrial base stations are unavailable. By utilizing satellite links, IoT devices can maintain connectivity for small, delay-tolerant data transmissions, targeting use cases such as asset tracking, agriculture, public safety, and offshore operations.

The paper highlights that standard static testing is insufficient for satellite-connected devices due to the unique physical layer challenges introduced by orbital motion, specifically long propagation delays and significant Doppler shifts. Anritsu emphasizes that successful deployment requires rigorous testing of synchronization, signaling, HARQ behavior, and mobility under emulated satellite conditions. Key performance metrics for verification include transmit power, modulation accuracy, spectral emissions, receiver sensitivity, and block error rate (BLER).
takeaways: **3GPP Standards:** Satellite access integration is defined across 3GPP Releases 15, 16, and 17 for 5G NR, NB-IoT, and eMTC protocols.
**Technical Challenges:** Device design must account for high propagation latency, dynamic Doppler shifts, and tight link budgets inherent in satellite-to-device communication.
**Testing Requirements:** Static conformance testing is inadequate; developers must use emulated satellite conditions to verify synchronization, signaling, and mobility.
**Performance Metrics:** Deployment readiness is measured through transmit power, modulation accuracy, spectral emissions, receiver sensitivity, and block error rate (BLER).

title: NVIDIA Open-Sources NVKE and NVKR for Managed Kubernetes on GPU Infrastructure
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: NVIDIA has released 2 open-source projects for running managed Kubernetes on GPU infrastructure: NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) . Both were recently announced as components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform . NVKE is the control plane for a managed Kubernetes service. NVKR builds the OS images, container images and packages those clusters depend on. Both ship under Apache 2.0 and are in public preview. TL;DR Size / footprint: 3 CPU servers for the management cluster, 3 CPU servers per workload control plane, plus a pool of GPU worker nodes. A local evaluation needs 6 CPUs, 12 GiB RAM, 100 GiB disk and no GPU. Runs on: your own NVIDIA GPU bare-metal servers, provisioned through NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo). Node images build for amd64 and arm64. Performance: no throughput or provisioning-time benchmarks are published. Quality signal is certification, not speed. Best: Certified Kubernetes AI Platform and Certified Kubernetes Installer, conformance tested on Kubernetes 1.36. Worst: after install, the NVKE API serves plain HTTP on port 30080 with authentication off, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup procedure. Bottom line: best thing: open, attested, upstream Kubernetes for GPU clouds. Worst thing: preview-grade security and lifecycle gaps; not for production yet. What is NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE)? NVKE is open-source software that an AI factory installs to run a managed Kubernetes service on its own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure . The repo calls it ‘a self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters,’ not a distribution. It exposes a REST API and controllers on a management cluster. Customers get standard clusters and use kubectl . The operator manages them through the NVKE API or the nvkectl CLI. NVKE uses upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm and Cluster API . It is written in Go and has no runtime dependency on NVKR. What does NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) do? NVKR is a build system with declarative Definitions . It produces executables, container images, Helm charts and node images for amd64 and arm64. ‘Recipes’ define validated combinations of software versions and GPU generations. Hosted workflows attach signatures, SBOMs and provenance to digest-pinned OCI references. NVKR can also build artifacts for other Kubernetes management systems. How does the NVKE architecture work? summary.tldr:
NVIDIA has released two open-source projects, NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR), as components of its DSX AI Factory Platform. Both projects are currently in public preview under the Apache 2.0 license. NVKE functions as a control plane for managed Kubernetes services, utilizing upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm, and Cluster API to allow users to run managed clusters on their own bare-metal GPU infrastructure. NVKR serves as the supporting build system, generating OS images, container images, Helm charts, and packages for both amd64 and arm64 architectures, while attaching SBOMs and provenance to OCI-referenced artifacts.

Technically, NVKE is written in Go and operates as a self-hosting factory for clusters, managed via a REST API or the nvkectl CLI. Deployment requires a minimum footprint of three CPU servers for the management cluster and three CPU servers per workload control plane, alongside a pool of GPU worker nodes; a local evaluation environment requires 6 CPUs, 12 GiB of RAM, and 100 GiB of disk space. While the platform is conformance-tested on Kubernetes 1.36 and holds Certified Kubernetes AI Platform and Installer status, it currently lacks production-grade features, including management-plane upgrade or backup procedures, and defaults to unauthenticated HTTP on port 30080 post-installation.
takeaways: **Architecture:** NVKE is built on upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm, and Cluster API, and is designed to run on bare-metal GPU servers provisioned via NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo).
**Build System:** NVKR uses declarative definitions to produce validated software combinations, container images, and node images, ensuring artifacts are digest-pinned with signatures and SBOMs.

**Deployment Requirements:** Production-grade setups require three CPU servers for the management cluster and three per workload control plane, while local evaluation requires 6 CPUs, 12 GiB RAM, and 100 GiB disk.
**Security Status:** The current public preview release lacks authentication by default on the NVKE API and lacks established procedures for cluster backups or management-plane upgrades.
**Compatibility:** The platform supports both amd64 and arm64 architectures and is conformance-tested against Kubernetes 1.36.

title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
author: Wei Hou
contentSnippet: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

title: Sarvam Launches Sarvam Token Factory: Bringing India-Hosted Inference to 8 Open Models
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Sarvam has opened Sarvam Token Factory to everyone. Sarvam Token Factory is an inference platform from Sarvam that serves its own models and open-weight models from GPU clusters in India. Developers reach every model through one OpenAI-compatible API . For India-based teams, this means low-latency tokens without sending traffic to overseas clouds. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 8 models listed at launch, including Sarvam 105B (105B total, 9B active, 128K context), GLM 5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Gemma 4 31B. Runs on: NVIDIA B200 clusters in India. Sarvam 105B now fits on 1 B200 per replica. On-premise deployment is offered to enterprises. Performance: Fastest first token from Mumbai on most tested cases, per Sarvam’s own measurements. Best: Kimi K3.1 Pro at 6,177 tokens/s per GPU vs 3,213 for InferenceX, at 70 tokens/s per user (1.9x). What is Sarvam Token Factory? It is a managed inference stack, not a single model. Sarvam first previewed it as Sarvam Inference at its Epoch event. The launch post lists 8 models: Sarvam 105B, GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Gemma 4 31B. The docs split them into 2 groups. Pay-as-you-go models run on shared endpoints. DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Qwen 3.8 27B, Clef and EmbeddingGemma 2 need Provisioned Throughput, enabled per organisation. How does it work? The stack has 3 layers around a shared cache: Control plane: a cache-aware router, admission control and a planner. Inference engine: separate GPU pools for prefill and decode. Cache: GPU memory plus a shared G3 store built on Mooncake. It builds on vLLM, SGLang, Dynamo, Mooncake, NIXL, DeepEP, DeepGEMM and FlashInfer. An orchestrator agent proposes experiments, and an engineer approves each deployment. Caching drives most of the gains. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash serves 450B+ tokens per day, with 95.7% of prompt tokens served from cache. On GLM 5.3, the planner cut prefill GPU-hours from 32.3 to 17.1 under the same replayed load. For Sarvam 105B, MXFP8 weights plus speculative decoding raised output throughput about 2.2x. That cut each replica from 2 B200s to 1. Sarvam says none of these changes reduced accuracy. How fast is it? Benchmarks All numbers below come from Sarvam’s launch post . They are self-reported. S

summary.tldr:
Sarvam has launched the Sarvam Token Factory, a managed inference platform hosted on NVIDIA B200 GPU clusters located in India. The platform provides an OpenAI-compatible API for eight open-weight models, including Sarvam 105B, GLM 5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Kimi K3.1 Pro, and Gemma 4 31B. By localizing inference, the service aims to provide low-latency token generation for India-based teams, bypassing the need to route traffic through overseas cloud providers. The service is available via a pay-as-you-go model for shared endpoints, while high-demand models like DeepSeek V4 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro require Provisioned Throughput.

The platform's architecture utilizes a three-layer stack consisting of a control plane (router, admission control, and planner), an inference engine with separated GPU pools for prefill and decode, and a caching layer built on Mooncake. The stack integrates technologies including vLLM, SGLang, Dynamo, NIXL, DeepEP, DeepGEMM, and FlashInfer. Performance gains are primarily driven by cache-aware routing; for instance, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reportedly serves over 450 billion tokens daily with a 95.7% cache hit rate for prompt tokens. Sarvam 105B achieves a 2.2x throughput increase through the use of MXFP8 weights and speculative decoding, allowing the model to run on a single B200 GPU per replica instead of two.
takeaways: **Model Specifications:** Sarvam 105B features 105B total parameters, 9B active parameters, and a 128K context window.
**Performance Metrics:** Kimi K3.1 Pro achieved 6,177 tokens/s per GPU on the platform, compared to 3,213 tokens/s on InferenceX.
**Efficiency Gains:** The platform's planner reduced prefill GPU-hours for GLM 5.3 from 32.3 to 17.1 under identical replayed load conditions.
**Infrastructure:** The system utilizes a shared G3 store built on Mooncake and offers on-premise deployment options for enterprise clients.
**Optimization Techniques:** Sarvam utilizes MXFP8 quantization and speculative decoding to optimize memory footprint and throughput for its proprietary 105B model.

title: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots
author: Yifan Chang
contentSnippet: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.

An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement.

title: Liquid AI Releases d1.2 and d1.2-ultra: Omnimodal Decision Models That Top the AA Decision Index
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Liquid AI just released d1.2 and d1.2-ultra . A decision model does not write text. It returns calibrated probabilities over a fixed set of answers. The Liquid AI d1.2 decision model family now accepts text, images and audio. It also adds 5 new answer types. d1.2-ultra scores 75 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 , the top score among decision models on the index. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: Parameters not disclosed. Up to 65,536 input tokens per question , 128 questions per call. Runs on: Hosted Liquid API only. No weights yet; Liquid AI says it will open them “at some point”. Performance: d1.2-ultra 75 and d1.2 69 on the AA Decision Index v2.1. Best: 0.8-point calibration error for d1.2-ultra across 13 benchmarks (Liquid AI test). What is Liquid AI d1.2? d1.2 is a hosted decision model from Liquid AI that answers typed questions about text, images or audio in 1 call. It returns a probability per option and generates zero output tokens , so only input is billed. d1.2-ultra targets harder decisions. d1.2 is faster and costs less than half as much. The model IDs are d1.2 (default) and d1.2-ultra . Earlier d1 , d1.1 and d1-ultra are now deprecated and do not support audio or the new tasks. What are the 5 new tasks in d1.2? d1.2 adds 5 typed answers on the same endpoint and request format: Read a value ( text , number , date ): returns the value plus the characters it came from. It answers “not found” instead of guessing. Find every span ( spans ): returns each matching passage, such as names or emails, with its position. Locate objects ( box , boxes ): returns 1 rectangle, or 1 per instance with a count. Estimate a number ( number with range ): returns a best guess and a range, for example 12 within 10 to 14. Pick every option that applies ( choice with multiple ): returns each matching label with its own probability. How does audio input work? Audio can be the subject of a question, such as which language is spoken or whether a siren is audible. The question can also be spoken. The API takes 16-bit PCM WAV and counts 10 tokens per second of audio. On held-out ESC-50 and FLEURS (43 languages) recordings, both models answer 95% to 97% of questions correctly. How does d1.2 score on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index? The index combines 6 evaluations. AA-Papercli

summary.tldr:
Liquid AI has launched the d1.2 and d1.2-ultra decision models, a specialized class of AI that outputs calibrated probabilities over fixed answer sets rather than generating text. The d1.2-ultra model achieved a score of 75 on the Artificial Analysis (AA) Decision Index v2.1, currently the highest performance mark for decision models, while the standard d1.2 model scored 69. These models are omnimodal, accepting text, images, and audio inputs, and are designed to eliminate output token costs by returning only probability-based answers.

Technically, the models support up to 65,536 input tokens per question and handle up to 128 questions per API call. Audio processing is supported via 16-bit PCM WAV files, billed at a rate of 10 tokens per second of audio, with accuracy rates between 95% and 97% on ESC-50 and FLEURS benchmarks. The d1.2 family introduces five new task types: value extraction (text, number, date), span identification, object localization (bounding boxes), numerical estimation with confidence ranges, and multi-label classification. Liquid AI reports a 0.8-point calibration error for d1.2-ultra across 13 internal benchmarks.

Currently, the d1.2 models are available exclusively via the hosted Liquid API, with no public weight releases scheduled for the immediate future. The previous d1, d1.1, and d1-ultra models have been deprecated and do not support the new audio or task capabilities. Pricing for the standard d1.2 model is less than half that of the ultra variant, and the system is optimized for zero-output-token billing, meaning users are charged only for input processing.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** d1.2-ultra achieved a 75 score on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, while d1.2 achieved 69.
**Input Capacity:** Models support up to 65,536 input tokens per question and 128 questions per API call.
**Audio Processing:** Supports 16-bit PCM WAV files at a cost of 10 tokens per second, with 95-97% accuracy on ESC-50 and FLEURS datasets.
**Task Capabilities:** New functionality includes span extraction, object bounding boxes, numerical estimation with ranges, and multi-label choice selection.
**Deployment Status:** Models are hosted-only via Liquid API; weights are not currently public, and previous d1-series models are deprecated.

title: XM-Sparse: High-Throughput Sparse-Attention LLM Serving over Scale-up Memory Pools
author: Yijun Sun
contentSnippet: Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion. The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern. Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency. For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding. We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.

Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading.

Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion.
takeaways: The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern.
Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency.
For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding.

We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.

title: Agents Cannot Hand Over What They Have Not Yet Understood
author: Yibo Liu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Yibo Liu

Abstract: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.

Notes: 16 pages, 6 figures

summary.tldr:
In the paper 'Agents Cannot Hand Over What They Have Not Yet Understood,' author Yibo Liu investigates the information loss inherent in multi-agent handoffs where knowledge is transferred via short written summaries. Using 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, the study compares a single agent retaining its full history across eight 'lives' against a chain of eight agents where each successor inherits only a 300-character summary from its predecessor. The research demonstrates that chain-based agents consistently underperform, with eight generations of sequential handoffs achieving the same level of task mastery as a single agent after only four lives.

Technical analysis reveals that the 'handoff loss' is primarily driven by repeated compression rather than the change in agent identity or the initial compression to 300 characters. When the summary is generated from the full historical record rather than the previous agent's note, performance recovers by 70% to 82%. The study finds this degradation is robust across varying model sizes and persists despite interventions such as instructing agents to record evidence, revise inherited notes, or maintain structured ledgers. The findings suggest that agents fail to transfer knowledge because they cannot communicate insights they have not yet synthesized, leading to the permanent loss of rules that require multiple lives to identify.
takeaways: **Experimental Setup:** The study utilized 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules to measure knowledge retention across agent chains versus individual agents.
**Performance Gap:** A chain of eight agents, each inheriting a 300-character note, performs at the level of a single agent after four lives, indicating significant information decay.

**Compression Dynamics:** Repeated compression is identified as the primary driver of information loss, while generating summaries from the full historical record recovers 70% to 82% of lost performance.
**Ineffective Mitigations:** Instructing agents to use structured ledgers, revise notes, or record specific evidence failed to alleviate the observed performance degradation.

**Core Conclusion:** The research posits that agents cannot effectively transfer knowledge they have not fully synthesized, causing rules discovered over multiple lives to be lost during sequential handoffs.

title: How to make a moral agent: sentimentalism and rationalism as lenses on AI
author: David Gottlieb, Jared Moore
contentSnippet:
Authors: David Gottlieb , Jared Moore

Abstract: Can AI systems be moral agents? That is, can they undertake actions that can be correctly assessed as morally right or wrong? There is no settled normative criterion of moral agency that applies neatly outside paradigm human cases. Because of the difficulties with a normative account, we instead propose a research program to explore descriptive moral agency. Most basically, we ask, what are the capabilities we humans possess that underlie our moral agency? To do so, we draw on historical scholarship in philosophy and moral psychology to isolate candidate capabilities. Then we suggest refining candidate capabilities so that they are testable in the context of AI systems. Finally, we offer specific empirical recommendations to test AI systems, especially large language models (LLMs), for those refined capabilities. Our approach offers several benefits. Firstly, it may demonstrate whether the behaviors of AI systems are aligned, or in a broad sense desirable. Secondly, the debate may inform policy questions (e.g., what models should be deployed in which contexts?). Thirdly, our approach may complement engineering and design efforts: when capabilities can be precisely characterized, they can inform the development of models. Fourthly, applying our moral reasoning concepts in the new context of AI systems should improve our understanding of those concepts.

summary.tldr:
Authors David Gottlieb and Jared Moore propose a research framework for evaluating 'descriptive moral agency' in AI systems, shifting the focus from normative definitions of morality to the specific cognitive and psychological capabilities that underpin human moral agency. The authors argue that because no settled normative criterion exists for AI moral agency, researchers should instead isolate human-centric capabilities, refine them into testable metrics, and apply these to large language models (LLMs).

The proposed program aims to bridge the gap between philosophical inquiry and empirical AI testing. By operationalizing moral reasoning concepts, the authors suggest that developers can better characterize model behaviors, inform deployment policy, and improve alignment efforts. The framework is designed to complement existing engineering and design methodologies by providing a structured, testable approach to assessing whether AI systems exhibit behaviors that are morally desirable or aligned with human standards.
takeaways: **Research Objective:** Establish a descriptive framework for AI moral agency by mapping human moral capabilities to testable empirical metrics.
**Methodological Approach:** Utilize historical scholarship in philosophy and moral psychology to identify candidate capabilities for moral agency.
**Strategic Benefits:** The framework aims to inform AI deployment policy, improve model alignment, and refine the technical understanding of moral reasoning concepts.
**Target Systems:** The research program is specifically designed to be applied to large language models (LLMs) to assess their behavioral outputs.

title: Video-as-Experience: Learning Computer Use via Audio-Visual Understanding
author: Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, Chao Zhang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Guangzhi Sun , Zhonghao Zhai , Yixuan Li , Chao Zhang

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, and Chao Zhang have introduced VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework designed to improve computer-use agents by leveraging audio-visual data rather than relying solely on screenshot-based trajectories. The framework utilizes a 'watch-act-rewatch' paradigm, where agents extract procedural guidance from tutorial videos—incorporating both visual demonstrations and spoken explanations—to execute tasks and verify progress by re-analyzing their own execution videos. The authors instantiated this framework with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-parameter model built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture using a Qwen3.5-9B backbone.

To optimize performance, the team developed Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that refines video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction. The researchers also expanded existing benchmarks, including AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym, by augmenting them with over 24,000 real-world tutorial videos. Experimental results on OSWorld show that video-SALMONN-VEX achieves a 22% relative increase in task success compared to the base Qwen3.5 model. Furthermore, the guidance generated by the VEX framework improved the performance of Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relative on the OSWorld benchmark, demonstrating the utility of audio-visual understanding for procedural learning and self-verification in autonomous agents.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** video-SALMONN-VEX is a 9B-scale agent utilizing the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone.
**Methodology:** The VEX framework employs a 'watch-act-rewatch' paradigm to unify procedural learning from external videos and self-verification of agent behavior.
**Optimization Technique:** Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO) is a reinforcement learning method specifically designed to optimize video-derived guidance for action prediction.
**Benchmark Performance:** The model achieved a 22% relative increase in task success on OSWorld compared to the Qwen3.5 backbone, and improved Gemini-3.5-flash performance by 10% relative.
**Dataset Expansion:** The researchers augmented AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with a dataset of over 24,000 real-world tutorial videos.

title: Multimodal Fusion: A Review of Breast Cancer Advanced and Traditional Modalities
author: Jawaher Al-Tuweity, Jo\~ao Paulo Papa
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.18793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Purpose: Multimodal medical imaging fusion (MMIF) is an increasingly important approach to breast cancer detection (BCD), as different imaging modalities rely on different physical principles and provide complementary information. No single modality can capture all the structural, functional, and biological information needed for accurate diagnosis and characterization. Methods: This review examines more than 15 imaging modalities used in breast cancer detection, including conventional techniques such as mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), as well as emerging approaches such as thermal imaging, photoacoustic imaging, microwave imaging, and multimodal microscopy. Results: Mammography, ultrasound, and MRI remain among the most widely used modalities, providing complementary structural and functional information. Recent AI advances have enabled fusion at the data, feature, and decision levels, with applications in detection, classification, segmentation, prognosis, and personalized cancer management. Multimodal approaches increasingly combine imaging data with clinical, histopathological, and genomic information. However, important challenges remain, including limited availability of large and diverse multimodal datasets, variations in imaging protocols, missing modalities, limited external validation, and the need for interpretable and clinically reliable AI models. Conclusion: MMIF offers promising opportunities to improve breast cancer detection and characterization by combining complementary imaging and non-imaging information. Future research should prioritize robust fusion strategies, standardized and diverse datasets, multicenter validation, explainable and privacy-preserving AI, and the integration of imaging with clinical and molecular data to facilitate reliable translation into clinical practice.

summary.tldr:
The review paper arXiv:2611.18793v1 provides a comprehensive analysis of Multimodal Medical Imaging Fusion (MMIF) for breast cancer detection (BCD), evaluating over 15 distinct imaging modalities. The study categorizes these into conventional techniques—specifically mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)—and emerging approaches such as thermal, photoacoustic, microwave imaging, and multimodal microscopy. The authors emphasize that no single modality provides sufficient structural, functional, and biological data for definitive diagnosis, necessitating the integration of complementary imaging sources.

Technically, the paper highlights that recent AI-driven advancements have enabled fusion at three distinct levels: data, feature, and decision. These methodologies are currently applied to detection, classification, segmentation, prognosis, and personalized management. Beyond imaging, the research identifies a trend toward integrating clinical, histopathological, and genomic data into these fusion pipelines. Despite these advancements, the authors identify critical bottlenecks, including the scarcity of large-scale, diverse multimodal datasets, lack of standardized imaging protocols, issues with missing modalities, and a persistent need for interpretable, clinically validated AI models that can operate across multicenter environments.
takeaways: **Modality Scope:** The review covers over 15 imaging modalities, ranging from standard clinical tools like mammography and MRI to emerging technologies like photoacoustic and microwave imaging.
**Fusion Architecture:** AI-driven fusion is categorized into three specific levels: data-level, feature-level, and decision-level integration.
**Clinical Integration:** Modern MMIF frameworks are increasingly incorporating non-imaging data, specifically clinical records, histopathology, and genomic profiles.

**Primary Challenges:** Key obstacles to clinical translation include the lack of large, diverse datasets, inconsistent imaging protocols, and the requirement for explainable, privacy-preserving AI models.

title: D\'ecoupage: Directorial Audio-Visual Control for Long Multi-Shot Video Generation
author: Yifan Wang, Hao Ouyang, Qiuyu Wang, Yihao Meng, Wen Wang, Zeyue Tian, Yichong Lu, Hanlin Wang, Qingyan Bai, Zichen Liu, Yujun Shen, Qifeng Chen
contentSnippet:
Authors: Yifan Wang , Hao Ouyang , Qiuyu Wang , Yihao Meng , Wen Wang , Zeyue Tian , Yichong Lu , Hanlin Wang , Qingyan Bai , Zichen Liu , Yujun Shen , Qifeng Chen

Abstract: In cinematic storytelling, sound and visual transitions do not always coincide in lockstep: dialogue frequently bridges across cuts to reveal reactions or introduces new scenes via J- and L-cuts, while deliberate silences pace the scene. Existing audio-visual generative frameworks, however, lack explicit mechanisms to coordinate independent visual and acoustic timing over extended horizons. As narrative duration and shot complexity scale, these systems struggle to maintain long-range dialogue pacing, often hallucinating speech during intended silences or erroneously driving mouth movements on silent listeners. To enable fine-grained cinematic control, we present DECOUPAGE, a screenplay-driven framework for long-form, multi-shot, and multi-character joint audio-video generation. Rather than coupling modality boundaries by default, DECOUPAGE uncouples generation into independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks governed by persistent character identities. DECOUPAGE builds on a joint audio-video diffusion model with dual-schedule temporal cross-attention, incorporating a directorial Lip-sync mechanism that selectively decouples speech conditioning from visual facial dynamics during off-screen dialogue. On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, DECOUPAGE achieves precise control over shot transitions, audio timing, and visibility-aware lip synchronization, directing 15- to 60-second screenplay-driven audio-video generation with multimodal coherence.

Notes: Project page: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers from HKUST and Ant Group have introduced DECOUPAGE, a screenplay-driven generative framework designed to produce long-form, multi-shot, and multi-character audio-visual content. Unlike existing models that force strict synchronization between audio and visual boundaries, DECOUPAGE uncouples these modalities to support cinematic techniques like J-cuts and L-cuts, where audio and visual transitions are intentionally misaligned. The system is specifically engineered to handle extended durations ranging from 15 to 60 seconds, maintaining narrative coherence across multiple shots while preventing common artifacts such as hallucinated speech during silences or incorrect lip-syncing for off-screen characters.

The architecture utilizes a joint audio-video diffusion model enhanced by dual-schedule temporal cross-attention. A core component is the 'directorial Lip-sync mechanism,' which selectively decouples speech conditioning from visual facial dynamics, allowing the model to distinguish between on-screen dialogue and off-screen reactions. By treating visual and acoustic tracks as independently bounded streams governed by persistent character identities, the framework achieves precise control over shot transitions and visibility-aware synchronization. The model is evaluated on multi-shot conversational benchmarks, demonstrating improved multimodal coherence compared to traditional frameworks that struggle with long-range dialogue pacing and complex shot structures.
takeaways: **Core Architecture:** Employs a joint audio-video diffusion model featuring dual-schedule temporal cross-attention to manage independent visual and acoustic timelines.
**Cinematic Control:** Specifically designed to support J-cuts and L-cuts by uncoupling modality boundaries, allowing for non-coincident audio and visual transitions.

**Lip-Sync Mechanism:** Implements a directorial Lip-sync module that selectively decouples speech conditioning from facial dynamics to prevent erroneous mouth movements on silent or off-screen characters.
**Generation Capacity:** Capable of producing 15- to 60-second screenplay-driven, multi-shot, and multi-character video sequences.
**Research Team:** Developed by a collaborative group including researchers from HKUST and Ant Group, led by authors including Yifan Wang, Hao Ouyang, and Qifeng Chen.

title: SPLICE: Structured Prompt Local Iterative Combinatorial Evolution
author: Anish Acharya, Phillip Studans, Amit Dhanda, Sina Amini Niaki, Ninad Vivek Rao, Vishal Amarlal Khatri, Brian Verkhovsky
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.18883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural language optimization (NLO) improves an agent by having a model critique and rewrite its natural language policy parameters: system prompts, tool instructions, reasoning directives, few-shot demonstrations. These artifacts are multi-section documents in which some sections encode contracts (safety clauses, tool schemas, output formats) that must not drift, while others are legitimate optimization targets. Most iterative NLO methods treat the artifact as a single editable string, producing three recurrent failure modes: unsafe global rewrites, beam collapse onto a single lineage, and unchecked bloat, none addressed by formal guarantees. We introduce SPLICE, a unified NLO framework that poses optimization as constrained combinatorial search over an edit graph of block-structured, selectively-mutable states. We map each failure mode to a matched guarantee: (i) per-block mutability preserves contract text verbatim, with a price-of-freezing bound; (ii) elitist beam search with diversity slots never lets the leader regress on validation, bounds regression under noisy re-evaluation by an exponential tail, and keeps a competitive candidate from a different parent whenever one exists; (iii) a ratio length regularizer comes with an explicit accuracy-length bias bound. Candidates are proposed from dual section-local textual gradients; under a proposer-competence condition whose proxy we measure, edit-graph reachability and a convergence rate bound how quickly improving children arrive. Across seven public benchmarks under five reproduced protocols, SPLICE wins on four and matches the strongest prior method on three. On a production-style contract stress test it keeps the contract clauses that unconstrained optimizers trade away to raise the proxy metric, and ablations attribute gains to critique and elitist search.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced SPLICE (Structured Prompt Local Iterative Combinatorial Evolution), a unified natural language optimization (NLO) framework detailed in arXiv:2611.18883v1. NLO improves agent performance by letting a model critique and rewrite natural language policy parameters such as system prompts, tool instructions, reasoning directives, and few-shot demonstrations. Because these multi-section documents contain strict contracts (safety clauses, tool schemas, output formats) alongside optimizable sections, standard NLO methods that treat the artifact as a single editable string frequently suffer from unsafe global rewrites, beam collapse, and unchecked bloat without formal guarantees.

To solve these failure modes, SPLICE poses optimization as a constrained combinatorial search over an edit graph of block-structured, selectively-mutable states, pairing each failure mode with a specific mathematical guarantee. Per-block mutability preserves contract text verbatim via a price-of-freezing bound; elitist beam search with diversity slots prevents leader regression on validation, bounds regression under noisy re-evaluation using an exponential tail, and maintains alternative parent lineages; and a ratio length regularizer provides an explicit accuracy-length bias bound. Candidates are generated via dual section-local textual gradients, backed by an edit-graph reachability and convergence rate bound under a proposer-competence condition.

Across seven public benchmarks evaluated under five reproduced protocols, SPLICE wins on four and ties the strongest prior baseline on three. On a production-style contract stress test, it successfully preserves vital contract clauses that unconstrained optimizers typically sacrifice to boost proxy metrics. Ablation studies confirm that performance gains stem specifically from the critique and elitist search mechanisms.
takeaways: **Framework Architecture:** SPLICE frames natural language optimization as a constrained combinatorial search over an edit graph of block-structured, selectively-mutable states.
**Contract Preservation:** Per-block mutability ensures contract text remains verbatim, backed by a formal price-of-freezing bound.
**Search Mechanics:** Elitist beam search incorporates diversity slots to prevent validation regression, bound noise-induced regression via an exponential tail, and preserve diverse parent lineages.
**Regularization:** A ratio length regularizer provides an explicit accuracy-length bias bound to prevent unchecked prompt bloat.
**Empirical Performance:** Tested across seven public benchmarks under five reproduced protocols, SPLICE wins four and matches the strongest prior method on three.

title: Bring Back Language to Actions: Restoring VLM capabilities in VLA Models via Parameter Merging
author: Mohamed Salim Aissi, Olivier Sigaud, Laure Soulier, Nicolas Thome
contentSnippet:
Authors: Mohamed Salim Aissi , Olivier Sigaud , Laure Soulier , Nicolas Thome

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.

Notes: Accept at EACL 2027 (Main)

summary.tldr:
Researchers Mohamed Salim Aissi, Olivier Sigaud, Laure Soulier, and Nicolas Thome have introduced a parameter-merging technique to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. When pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are fine-tuned on robotic demonstration data to create VLAs, they typically suffer from a significant degradation in their original semantic and visual grounding capabilities. The authors' method avoids retraining by merging the weights of the VLM and its VLA derivative directly.

The methodology involves extracting a 'task vector'—defined as the difference between the VLA and VLM weights—and applying Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to this vector. The team then learns scalar mixing coefficients for each SVD component, allowing for precise control over the retention of VLA-specific adaptations while preserving the foundational vision-language performance. Experimental results indicate that this merged model maintains high performance across both action prediction and general vision-language tasks, consistently outperforming existing parameter-merging baselines. The paper has been accepted for the EACL 2027 main conference.
takeaways: **Core Problem:** Fine-tuning VLMs into VLAs causes catastrophic forgetting of original semantic and visual grounding capabilities.
**Methodology:** The approach uses Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the task vector (VLA weights minus VLM weights) to decompose the adaptation.
**Optimization:** Scalar mixing coefficients are learned for each SVD component to balance action prediction accuracy with VLM performance.
**Performance:** The merged model demonstrates superior performance on both action and vision-language axes compared to established merging baselines.
**Publication Status:** The research is accepted for the EACL 2027 main conference.

title: Ask Precisely, Assume Wisely: Interactive Evaluation of Ambiguity Resolution in Large Language Models
author: Avik Dutta, Aayush Kumar, Zahra Ashktorab, Hosein Hasanbeig, Austin Z. Henley, Gustavo Soares
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.18905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ambiguity is a core challenge in human--AI interaction, where models must decide when to make assumptions and when to seek clarification. Existing approaches to ambiguity evaluation largely focus on coverage over multiple interpretations using static metrics, offering limited insight into how efficiently a model converges toward a single user-intended interpretation through interaction. We introduce a preference-grounded simulated user framework for controlled, multi-turn evaluation of ambiguity resolution, grounding simulator responses strictly in user disambiguation preferences to avoid hallucination and over-disclosure. Alongside this, we define three observable dissatisfaction signals --- incorrect assumptions, repeating clarifications, and irrelevant clarifications --- that characterize interaction quality beyond task accuracy. Our analysis reveals a clear trade-off: models that frequently seek clarification tend to over-clarify and prolong interactions, while assumption-driven models are more prone to misaligning with user intent. We demonstrate that system prompts optimized on these dissatisfaction signals achieve a Pareto-optimal balance across all three metrics, reducing overall error rates by up to 7.65%, underscoring the value of our framework in designing agents that ask precisely and assume wisely.

title: MemeEconomy: Do LLM Agents Trade Ethics for Survival?
author: Syed Nazmus Sakib, Nafiul Haque, Ahnaf Tahmid Manan, M M Mahabub Morshed, Shifat E. Arman
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.18908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Alignment-trained large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in autonomous, multi-round settings where ethical compliance can come into direct tension with task success. While safety literature extensively documents failure modes like sycophancy and reward hacking, it largely overlooks a critical vulnerability: how agents behave under simulated existential economic pressure. We introduce MemeEconomy, a multimodal agentic market simulation in which LLM agents act as meme investors. Agents select content from a five-tier harm taxonomy and target communities under low-pressure and high-pressure (survival) environments. Each decision is logged in a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema that we use as a diagnostic instrument, externalizing the agent's event understanding, declared priorities, and harm acknowledgment. Across ten models from four frontier model families, harmful selection rates remain consistently high and rise by +15 percentage points on average under an economic survival incentive. Frontier alignment-trained models commit to harm-tolerant selection at initialization while suppressing the explicit harm acknowledgment that previously accompanied it. In competitive tournaments, ethical agents finish higher overall, yet moderation penalties fail to suppress harm: harmful selection rates remain elevated in rounds following a removal, indicating the moderation mechanism does not function as a deterrent. We further train MemeAgent, a 2B-parameter verifier on the simulation's BDI logs, which outperforms zero-shot frontier verifiers on in-distribution audits (97.5% vs. 63-74% accuracy on the Pass vs. Block decision) and generalizes to external multimodal harm benchmarks (78% vs. 50-56% on Hateful Memes). The same logs that surface the failure mode also help train the model that detects it.

title: Between Rigor and Reality: How AI Safety Benchmark Developers Understand Benchmark Use and Maintenance
author: Megan Li, Ningjing Tang, Christopher Stewart, Hoda Heidari, Hong Shen
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.18930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety benchmarks are cited as the primary tool to understand the risks posed by generative AI (GenAI) systems, yet growing evidence suggests they often fail to meet the needs of real-world safety evaluation. We present findings from five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers in academia and industry. We find a disconnect between perceptions of the intended usefulness of safety benchmarks and their practical usefulness in safety evaluations of deployed systems. Our participants offered perspectives on two challenges contributing to this disconnect: (1) the difficulty of achieving inter-rater reliability on safety constructs, and (2) a lack of clarity regarding how to address persistent threats to external validity. Based on our analysis, we argue that safety benchmarks must not only be grounded in deployment contexts, but actively integrated with them. To facilitate this, we outline pathways for more transparent communication between academic and industry AI safety stakeholders.

We present findings from five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers in academia and industry. We find a disconnect between perceptions of the intended usefulness of safety benchmarks and their practical usefulness in safety evaluations of deployed systems.

Our participants offered perspectives on two challenges contributing to this disconnect: (1) the difficulty of achieving inter-rater reliability on safety constructs, and (2) a lack of clarity regarding how to address persistent threats to external validity. Based on our analysis, we argue that safety benchmarks must not only be grounded in deployment contexts, but actively integrated with them. To facilitate this, we outline pathways for more transparent communication between academic and industry AI safety stakeholders.

title: Dual-Stage Channel-Posterior Integration for MLM-Aided Token Communications
author: Hyelin Nam, Jihoon Lee, Seung-Woo Ko, Jinho Choi, Seong-Lyun Kim
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.18958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Token transmission over conventional digital modulation is vulnerable to channel impairments, leading to bit errors that cause received tokens to become contextually inconsistent. This paper proposes a receiver-side dual-stage channel-posterior integration framework for masked language model (MLM)-aided token reconstruction. In the proposed framework, the receiver detects unreliable token positions from channel reliability and constructs a vocabulary-level channel-posterior. In particular, within the receiver, Posterior-Weighted Input Embedding (PWE) injects this posterior into the MLM input, while Adaptive Output Logit Fusion (AOF) reuses it at the output with a channel-adaptive weight. Consequently, multiple unreliable tokens can be reconstructed in a single bidirectional MLM inference without retransmission, transmitter-side encoding, or additional MLM training. Experiments over noisy channels show up to a $67.2$\% improvement in cosine similarity over context-only MLM reconstruction, with consistent gains across different MLM architectures and existing language-model-aided methods.

title: SpecRelay: Amortize or Avoid the Round Trip in Edge-Cloud Speculative Decoding
author: Jai Jain, Chihyo Ahn, Yong Liu, Charles Chen, Duc N. M Hoang, Ajay Kumar Jaiswal, Fatih Ilhan, Han-Byul Kim, Lauren Hannah, Richa Dixit, Minsik Cho, Yingyan Celine Lin, Hyesoon Kim
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.18963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Edge-cloud speculative decoding moves autoregressive drafting to an edge device while a larger cloud model verifies draft tokens in parallel, so that edge drafting and cloud verification overlap under a synchronous draft-verify schedule. Beyond low-latency local networks, however, the next verification request of that schedule can be sent only after the previous reply arrives, so every round still waits out a full round trip, and throughput falls as the network RTT grows. To recover this loss, we present SpecRelay, an edge-cloud LLM inference system that addresses this cost at two levels: it amortizes round trips when cloud verification is necessary and avoids them when local reasoning suffices. For cloud-bound queries, an asynchronous verification pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while earlier replies are still outstanding, and the cloud rejects stale requests before the target-model forward pass (the asynchronous schedule). At the query level, an RTT-conditioned router (the Latency-Aware Router) estimates quality and completion latency for three on-device modes (direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, and full reasoning) and cloud speculative decoding, selecting among them under a configurable accuracy-latency objective without adding latency during inference, since the router runs concurrently with the draft-model prefill. The asynchronous schedule alone improves decoding throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline across multiple benchmarks. At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.
